Let’s dive into Chapter 5: Knowing Both Sides—Understanding Your Own Style and That of Others.
Have you ever noticed how seeing yourself clearly—and really understanding the person across from you—can totally shift the outcome of a negotiation, a competition, or even just an everyday conversation?
That’s the heart of effective strategy: developing an honest awareness of both your own approach and the unique style of anyone you engage with.
Let’s start with yourself. True self-knowledge means being upfront about your strengths, your habits, and yes, even your blind spots.
So, how do you get there?
First, take a look back at your own history—your wins, your stumbles. Are there patterns that keep popping up? Maybe you shine when you’re improvising, or perhaps you’re more effective when you’ve got a detailed plan.
Then, notice what feels natural for you. Which methods give you energy, and which ones leave you drained or off-balance?
And don’t forget your values. What really drives your decisions? When you understand what matters most to you, you’ll make choices that feel right—even under pressure.
Now, let’s flip the perspective.
Understanding someone else’s style is just as crucial. Whether you’re facing a business rival, a sparring partner, or just navigating daily life, every person brings their own habits into the mix.
Want to get a read on them? Start by watching for behaviors that repeat, especially in different situations.
Listen closely—not just to what’s said, but the way it’s said. Sometimes, a shift in tone reveals more than the words themselves.
And stay alert for changes in mood or energy. These can signal a shift in their approach, or even a new strategy you might not expect.
Here’s something to remember: this isn’t about judging or labeling someone. It’s about seeing clearly, so you can respond with skill instead of reacting emotionally.
It takes empathy to step into someone else’s shoes—and just enough detachment to keep your judgment sharp.
Now, what if you could actually learn from the people you’re competing with?
Every opponent, every challenging colleague, can show you something new—a technique, a perspective, maybe even a way of thinking you hadn’t considered before.
This kind of openness dissolves the wall between “us” and “them,” turning every encounter into a learning opportunity.
Think about a skilled negotiator. They don’t just push their own agenda—they adapt, tailoring their approach to match the personality and goals of the person across the table.
Or imagine a martial artist who shifts tactics the moment they spot their opponent’s favorite move.
The principle is the same: by knowing both yourself and the other, you give yourself a real edge.
This approach also brings out humility and respect. Instead of seeing others as obstacles, you start to recognize them as fellow travelers—each with their own strengths, struggles, and stories.
Not only does this make you more effective, but it deepens every connection you make.
So, if you want to become more adaptable, more insightful, and more successful—no matter what you’re facing—start by truly knowing both sides.
It’s a practice that pays off in every field, and in every relationship.
